# 

# Abstract

Removal of megafauna, changes in land use and abandonment of traditional agriculture practices have led to habitat loss and fragmentation across Europe. Grasslands are among the most affected habitats in this regard. The dusky large blue (*Phengaris nausithous*) is a univoltine butterfly species inhabiting humid meadows. The species’ lifecycle depends on the availability of its foodplant *Sanguisorba officinalis* and *Myrmica* sp. host ants.

# 

# Introduction

Changes in land use have led to major biological degradation of the European landscapes during the past century (Konvicka et al., 2021; Munguira and Martin, 1999; van Strien et al., 2019). Historically, the Holocene removal of large herbivores has been functionally replaced with traditional agricultural and silvicultural practices, which maintained a heterogenic landscape matrix (Ellis et al., 2021). However, the abandonment of these practices and rapid intensification of land use has led to a homogenisation of the landscape matrix and a widespread habitat loss across much of Europe (Skorka et al., 2007; Warren et al., 2021).  
	Detailed monitoring of widespread landscape changes requires methods demanding high resource and time investments. Biological conservation therefore often utilizes proxies in the form of umbrella species. Butterflies are among the most popular umbrella groups due to their high susceptibility to changes in habitat distribution, quality and connectivity. The Lycaenid family of butterflies are often characterised by specific requirements of habitat quality and sufficient abundance of species’ plant host.   
The dusky large blue *Phengaris (=Maculinea) nausithous* (Bergstäasser, 1779\) is a well-studied lycaenid butterfly species commonly described as an umbrella species of European humid grasslands. As one of the target features in the Natura 2000 network established by the EU Habitats Directive, *P. nausithous* and its sibling taxon *P. teleius* became flagship species in European nature conservation (Kajzer-Bonk et al., 2013). Like the other species within the *Phengaris* genus, it is characterised by a peculiar life history with multiple interspecific interactions. *P. nausithous* females lay multiple eggs on the flowers of the great burnet *Sanguisorba officinalis* (L.). The larvae feed on the flower buds during the early stages of development with only one larva finishing its development on each flower bud. Late instars then fall on the ground and chemically attract the workers of their host ant species, which carry them into the ant nest. *P. nausithous* larvae actively prey on the ant brood at this stage. The main host species of *P. nausithous* is *Myrmica rubra* (Linnaeus, 1758), although the interspecific interactions are likely to vary locally depending on the ant species’ availability. Other *Myrmica* species, mainly *M. scabrinodis*, were also reported to be parasitized by the larvae when *M. rubra* nests were absent or present at low densities (Pech et al., 2007; Perez-Sanchez et al., 2020; Witek et al., 2008).  
Like most butterfly species in Europe, *P. nausithous* is widely described to occur in metapopulations requiring multiple habitat patches to survive in an area (Figurny-Puchalska et al., 2000; Nowicki et al., 2007; Vrabec et al., 2017). Metapopulation theory has become a paradigm in insect research and conservation over the past two decades (Hanski et al., 2000; Levins, 1969; Wahlberg et al., 2002). Driven by local extinction and colonisation events within the metapopulation system, the theory can be applied to presence-absence data for the individual habitat patches (Hanski, 1994; Hanski *et al.*, 2000; Thomas et al., 2011). Many insect species occupy naturally patchy landscapes shaped by the activity of large herbivores and abiotic factors (Konvicka *et al.*, 2021). Such environments are characterised by high rates of disturbance and changes in local conditions within habitat patches can often lead to the extinction of individual populations within the system (Betzholtz et al., 2007; Hanski, 1994; Warren *et al.*, 2021). Kajzer-Bonk et al. (2013) showed that metapopulation systems of *P. nausithous* are resistant even to major habitat disturbances. Furthermore, parasite infections within a population have been reported to cause cyclical changes in population abundances (John et al., 2021; Sliwinska et al., 2019). The population increases and declines can be also caused by both short- and long-term changes in climate. As a result, the availability of resources and connectivity of areas with suitable conditions determine the metapopulation dynamics and long-term survival of the species in fragmented landscapes.  
	The distribution of resources in patchy landscapes presents a major predictor of the persistence of individual populations within a metapopulation matrix (Betzholtz *et al.*, 2007; Hanski *et al.*, 2000; Nowicki *et al.*, 2007). Both host organisms required by *P. nausithous* for its life cycle inhabit structurally heterogenous humid grasslands maintained by low-intensity grazing or mowing (Johst et al., 2006; Skorka *et al.*, 2007; Thomas, 1984). The intensification of the management directly leads to declines in the *S. officinalis* abundance and destruction of *Myrmica* sp. microhabitat.   
	Dispersal affects the species’ ability to colonise new habitat patches as well as to maintain gene flow between already established populations*.* Avoiding inbreeding avoiding intraspecific competition*.* Metapopulation structure was also shown to decreases the risks associated with abundance fluctuations within individual populations (John *et al.*, 2021).   
	Previous studies aiming to determine the impact of individual resources have mostly applied the frequentist statistics approach and have been based either on evaluating species-habitat associations based on a single population or relatively small metapopulations systems (Kajzer-Bonk *et al.*, 2013; Korosi et al., 2012; Perez-Sanchez *et al.*, 2020). Furthermore, previous studies depended largely on intensive survey methods, hence limiting the area covered. This investigation aimed to use the Bayesian approach to estimate the effects of the host plant, area of habitat patch, and isolation of the site. Using prior ecological knowledge derived from already published research a metapopulation model was used to estimate the parameter values. The estimated parameter values were then used to determine the effects of food plant availability on the occupancy patterns of the metapopulation system.

# Materials and methods

## Study organism

Dusky large blue butterfly (*Phengaris nausithous*) is a univoltine species distributed across much of the Palearctic (Fric et al., 2007; Wynhoff et al., 2011). In Europe, *P. nausithous* is found mainly in central and eastern parts with an isolated population in the north of the Iberian Peninsula (Jubete and Roman, 2016; Romo et al., 2015). The species went extinct in parts of western Europe due to habitat loss caused by the cessation of grassland management but was recently successfully reintroduced to multiple sites in the region (Wynhoff et al., 2008). It is most abundant across the centre and the east of the continent (Fric *et al.*, 2007; Skorka *et al.*, 2007; Vrabec *et al.*, 2017).   
The larvae of *P. nausithous* are obligate feeders on flower buds of their foodplant *Sanguisorba officinalis* and pupae of their host ants, mainly *Myrmica rubra* (Perez-Sanchez et al., 2020; Thomas, 1984; Thomas and Elmes, 1998). While *S. officinalis* is easily identified in the field and its relative abundances can be estimated with minimal sampling effort, the identification of *Myrmica* sp. ants requires the collection of multiple individuals from the site. Furthermore, estimating the density of ant nests on a habitat patch was shown to require a considerably larger sampling effort than recording the presence of *P. nausithous* and *S.* officinalis (Jansen et al., 2012; Perez-Sanchez et al., 2020; Wynhoff et al., 2011). For this reason, the available host ant occurrence data are very likely to be incomplete and the presence of the host ants on the evaluated habitat patches would be falsely negative. The presence of the host ants was hence omitted in this study.

## Study area

The study was conducted on the territory of the Krivoklatsko Protected Landscape Area in the central Czech Republic (49°47’ N; 13°52’ E). The size of the territory is 628 km² with elevation ranging from 217 m to 616 m above sea level. The mean annual temperature is 7.6 °C and the mean annual precipitation is 7980 mm.  The geology of the area is a diverse combination of Protezoic volcanic rocks and Cambrian slates resulting in a naturally patchy matrix of habitats. The landscape is covered mainly by coniferous forests, grasslands, fields, and urban settlements. Krivoklatsko is divided by the Berounka river valley. The protection of the area has established in 1978 and is located in close proximity to the country’s capital. As a result, the territory has been studied historically and the development of the local landscapes is well understood.  
	Wet meadows with *Phengaris* habitat were located across the study area (Figure 1). Individual habitat patches are separated by various habitat types, creating a fragmented landscape regarding the requirements of the study species. Within the study area, 126 habitat patches were identified based on the distribution recorded during the Habitat Mapping Scheme (see below).

## Data acquisition, preparation and GIS

*P. nausithous* and *S. officinalis* occurrence data were obtained from the Species Occurrence Database of the Czech Republic. Data used in the analysis entered the database from two main sources. Long-term monitoring schemes with well-defined methodology were used as a primary data source. The dataset was complemented by random findings verified based on their authorship and provided evidence of correct species identification. Only validated findings thus entered the analysis. The dataset was further filtered to include only recent (\< 2009\) findings with precision \< 50 m to prevent errors in assorting the butterfly and foodplant presence to the individual habitat patches.  
	The distribution of the habitat patches was obtained from the Habitat Mapping Database of the Czech Republic (CR, 2020). The resource consists of georeferenced data on the distribution and quality of both natural habitats and those strongly affected by human cultivation. The nomenclature of the habitats follows the Habitat Catalogue of the Czech Republic transferrable to other widely recognised taxonomies (Chytrý et al., 2010). The Habitat Mapping Database is produced as a product of the nationwide Habitat Mapping Scheme and was originally designed for habitat monitoring based on the Habitats Directive. As part of the methodology, the country’s territory is divided into districts (n \= 3493\) with a 12-year update rate resulting in cca 8.3 % of habitats being revisited each year. Areas are further divided into segments Only data collected between 2009 and 2021 entered the analysis.  
	 Next, the habitat patches within the metapopulation system were chosen based on published research and preliminary analysis. Using the same taxonomy as Chytrý et al. (2010), mesic *Arrhenatherum* meadows, alluvial *Alopecurus* meadows, wet *Cirsium* meadows, and intermittently wet *Molinia* meadows were identified as potential habitats of *P. nausithous* since *S. officinalis* has been listed for them as a diagnostic species. Furthermore, intensively managed meadows were included in the selection as both *P. nausithous* and *S. officinalis* are commonly reported from them.  
	Data manipulation and data analysis were conducted using R (RCoreTeam, 2021). The spatial data were first analysed using the sf package (Pebesma, 2018). For each habitat patch, an intercept between itself and butterfly and plant occurrence data was used to retrieve presence-absence data for both variables. Neighbouring habitat patches with identical properties were merged. Area in hectares and the Euclidean distance matrix within the metapopulation system were calculated for the united habitat patches. For computational reasons, only patches larger than 5 hectares were considered in the analysis. 

## Model development

A Bayesian model was used to investigate the effects playing role in the metapopulation dynamics of *P. nausithous*.   
An occupancy matrix *S* was used to record changes in the state of individual habitat patches. Each row of the matrix represented an individual patch (n \= 126). Simulation time was set to 50 generations (${t}_{max}=50$) resulting in 50 columns of the matrix. The metapopulation model distinguished between two states (*extinct* and *occupied*) per habitat patch:  
$${S}_{i,t+1}=\{∼B\left({1, {p}_{i}}\right),  {S}_{i,t}=0 \left({extinct}\right)\ ∼B\left({1, {q}_{i}}\right),  {S}_{i,t}=1 \left({occupied}\right)\ $$

where ${S}_{i,t}$ is the occupancy state of the ith patch at the *t* time. If a patch was occupied, persistence likelihood was calculated. For a vacant habitat patch, the model calculates the probability of colonisation by any of the occupied patches.   
The parameter affecting the likelihood of persistence of an individual population (extinction event not taking place) was expressed as ${l}_{i}$ and consisted of several components: basal persistence (${a}_{0})$, presence of the foodplant on the habitat patch (${P}_{i}$), the effect of the foodplant on persistence (${a}_{1})$, the effect of the habitat patch area (${a}_{2}$), and area of the patch in hectares (${A}_{i}$). The parameter was calculated as a product of the listed components:  
$${l}_{i}={a}_{0}+{a}_{1}\times {P}_{i}+{a}_{2}\times {A}_{i}$$

The probability of the persistence (1 – the probability of extinction) of an individual population within a habitat patch was calculated as follows:  
$${q}_{i}= \frac{exp⁡({l}_{i})}{1+exp⁡({l}_{i})}$$

The parameter ${\Phi }_{i,j}$ affecting the probability of a colonisation event consisted of three components: basic rate of colonisation $({b}_{0}$), the effect of distance between two patches (${b}_{1}$), and the distance itself (${D}_{i,j}$):  
$${\Phi }_{i,j}={b}_{0}+{b}_{1}\times {D}_{i,j}$$

The likelihood of a vacant colony *i* being colonised by currently occupied colony *j* was described as:  
$${p}_{j→i}= \frac{exp⁡({\Phi }_{i})}{1+exp⁡({\Phi }_{i})}$$

The probability of successful colonisation of an individual habitat patch by any of the occupied sites in the system was calculated as the product of individual probabilities:  
$${p}_{i}=1-\prod\limits_{j=1}^{N}(1-{p}_{j→i})$$

This approach considers a product of the probabilities that an individual patch fails to be colonised. Subtraction of this product hence expresses the probability of a successful colonisation event.

## Model fitting

Using the prior distributions listed in Table 1 the parameter values were estimated from the model by JAGS software (Plummer, 2003\) using a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling algorithm (see Appendix I for the R code). The runjags package was used to deploy JAGS in the R interface (Denwood, 2016). Model convergence was assessed using the effective sample sizes and by visual evaluation of the trace plots (see Appendix II).

| Parameter | Prior value | Prior distribution |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Basal persistence (*a0*) | \-0.5 | $$N(0,\ 1)$$ |
| Host plant effect on persistence (*a1*) | 1.5 | $$N(0,\ 1)$$ |
| Patch area effect on persistence (*a2*) | 0.5 | $$N(0,\ 1)$$ |
| Basal rate of colonisation (*b0*) | 1 | $$N(0,\ 1)$$ |
| Effect of distance on colonisation  (*b1*) | \-0.005 | $$Gamma(0.005,0.005)$$ |

***Table 1:*** The list of parameters with associated prior values and distributions used in the JAGS model.

During the simulation, an occupancy vector was calculated for each patch using the frequency of the patch being occupied:  
$${poc}_{i}=\sum\limits_{}^{}\frac{{S}_{i,t}}{{t}_{max}-{t}_{min}+1}$$

The vector was then used to calculate the occupancy likelihood:   
$${Oc}_{i}=B({poc}_{i},1)$$

The resulting values were finally used by the JAGS model and confronted with simulated values:  
$${S}_{i,1}\ ~\ B(0.5,1)$$

## Investigating the effects of resource availability 

In the next step, the different scenarios of foodplant distribution across the network were explored. *S. officinalis* is one of the crucial resources required by the study organism. This was achieved by using the estimated posterior parameter values by the original model while manipulating the presence of the foodplant for each habitat patch individually.   
Simulated plant occurrence patterns in the metapopulation network were generated with various probabilities based on a binomial distribution. This was done for individual patches (${P}_{i}$) in the system:  
$${P}_{i}\ ~\ B(1,\ x)$$

with $x$ being the probability of *S. officinalis* presence within the patch and ranging from 0 to 1 with an 0.1 increment. The mean occupancy derived from the ${Oc}_{i}$ vector was then calculated for each scenario. Finally, the effect of the *S. officinalis* scarcity within the metapopulation matrix was analysed using GLM.

# Results

Out of the total of 126 habitat patches, 18 (14.3 %) were occupied by *P. nausithous* and *S. officinalis* was present in 21 (16.7 %) of them. Mean patch area in the study territory was 14.746 ha (n \= 126, SD \= 18.784). The estimated parameter values are presented in Table 2\. Given the mean patch area, the mean effect of the area component (${a}_{2}\times {A}_{i}$) was calculated to be 0.159.  
**Table 2:** Parameter values estimated using the JAGS model

| Notation | Parameter | Posterior median | Posterior mean | 95-percentiles |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| *a0* | The basal rate of persistence | 1.180 | 1.170 | \[0.662,1.681\] |
| *a1* | Host plant effect on persistence | 0.425 | 0.442 | \[-0.368,1.338\] |
| *a2* | Patch area effect on persistence | 0.0108 | 0.0108 | \[-0.00394,0.0259\] |
| *b0* | The basal rate of colonisation | \-1.091 | \-1.081 | \[-1.708, \-0.450\] |
| *b1* | Effect of distance on colonisation | \-0.00188 | \-0.00192 | \[-0.00116,-0.00269\] |

	The posterior parameter values were used to investigate occupancy patterns in the metapopulation system.

**Figure 2:** Simulated mean occupancy patterns using the parameter values estimated by the Bayesian model. The size of the circles is derived from the mean occupancy. Habitat patches with no occupancy recorded during the simulation are plotted in a triangular shape. 

The statistical analysis revealed a significant difference in the mean occupation values between initially occupied and vacant habitat patches (*W* \= 1415.5, *p* \= 0.002)(Fig. 4). However, the analysis did not reveal any significant differences between the patches with the presence of the food plant and sites with no *S. officinalis* records (*W* \= 1115, *p* \= 0.936).   
In the simulation of various foodplant distribution scenarios, the effect of *S. officinalis* scarcity was shown to significantly affect the mean occupancy of habitat patches (*R2* \= 0.648, *F*1,9 \= 16.53, *p* \= 0.003)(Fig. 5). 

**Figure 3:** *The effect of host plant scarcity across the habitat patches on the modelled mean occupancy.*

# Discussion

In this study, I estimated the relative contributions of several important parameters affecting the metapopulation dynamics of *Phengaris nausithous* using the Bayesian approach. The effects of the foodplant *S. officinalis* presence and the habitat patch area on population persistence were quantified  
The basal rate of persistence was greater than the combination of the host plant and patch area effects. Includes multiple effects. *S. officinalis* cover. Host ant nest availability.   
Isolated populations go extinct. Cyclical changes in butterfly populations. One of the isolated populations is located within a Natura 2000 site (Rakovnik – za koupalistem). *P. nausithous* is the sole target feature of the site. Increase connectivity by introducing stepping stones. Road verges have been often hypothesised to facilitate the dispersal of *P. nausithous* in fragmented landscapes such as Krivoklatsko. Relatively low cost.  
Local hydrological conditions. The occupancy pattern simulated using the posterior parameter values shows a strong newly established population in proximity to the Berounka river. Alluvial meadows are widely reported to be among the preferred habitats of *P. nausithous*.  
Effects of management.  
Performance of the Euclidean distance as a predictor of colonisation likelihood. A fragmented landscape where habitat patches are often separated by forest and similar barriers the species cannot pass.    
Information on the minimal required area of a habitat patch, management of the foodplant or a requirement of stepping-stone introduction to improving connectivity within the metapopulation.
